Our framework seeks to establish vulnerability monoculture as a measurable target for a more wholistic adversarial evaluation of model populations.

title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor
authors: Maosen Zhang; Jianshuo Dong; Yutong Zhang; Jie Zhang; Tianwei Zhang; Han Qiu
abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.

title: Humans Correct Their Judgments Through Debate, but Weaker AI Models Do Not
authors: Maria Victoria Carro; Denise Alejandra Mester; Facundo Nieto; Oscar Agustin Stanchi; Guido Ernesto Bergman; Giovanni Franco Gabriel Marrafini; Trinidad Borrell; Guido Freire; Joaquin Salvador Machulsky; Mario Alejandro Leiva; Ana Lopez; Nicolas Spinelli; Luca Nicolas Forziati Gangi; Eitan Sprejer; Federico Barrera Lemarchand; Gerardo Simari; Maria Vanina Martinez
abstract: How can we effectively oversee AI systems that surpass human intelligence? AI Safety via Debate proposes that two AI systems argue opposing positions and a judge, either a human or a weaker model, decides which is correct. By facilitating supervisors in providing high-quality training signals, debate aims to encourage truthful and safe behavior from AI systems whose capabilities exceed our own. However, human judgment is not neutral: people often rely on biases which advanced AI systems may learn to exploit. Drawing on insights from collective intelligence and social cognition, this paper investigates whether debate can guide human and LLM supervisors toward the truth despite their prior beliefs. We evaluate several protocol configurations. We also explore setups inspired by the wisdom of the crowd such as the number and diversity of judges, as well as interaction mechanisms including deliberation and voting. Overall, we find that debate increases accuracy relative to prior beliefs for human judges, whereas the consultancy baseline, in which a single expert argues for one answer, does not. For weaker language models, however, the results are mixed: debate provides no comparable gains in most settings and can even reduce accuracy. Among multi-judge protocols, weighted voting produces the highest accuracy for human supervisors, whereas for LLMs none of them significantly improves group accuracy, even as the number of judges increases. Notably, the behavior of minority judges in non-diverse deliberation protocols suggests that, under symmetric settings, incorrect positions could be more persuasive than correct ones. These findings support debate as a viable path toward scalable human oversight, but cast doubt on its benefits for weaker AI supervisors, raising concerns about fully automated training and control pipelines in high-stakes settings.

title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems
authors: Wendy Zheng; Liang Wu; Yinhan He; Mayank Darbari; Jundong Li; Liangjie Hong
abstract: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.

title: Your Token Is Gone: A Token-Consumption Countermeasure for Disrupting LLM-Based Scam Systems
authors: Fudu Xing; Kailong Wang; Tianlong Yu
abstract: LLM-based scam systems increasingly combine adaptive dialogue, persistent context, external tools, and multi-agent coordination to automate personalized fraud. These capabilities also create a resource dependency: every reasoning step, model call, and coordination round incurs inference cost. We present TokenTrap, a resource-oriented defense that redirects suspected scam systems toward benign, low-value computation while withholding credentials, payments, and other exploitable information. TokenTrap combines three components: an architecture-specific token-task library, a router that selects among single-agent, hierarchical, and flat multi-agent workflows, and a bounded anti-guardrail strategy that varies task presentation while enforcing token, round, time, and safety limits. Across 50-round traces, TokenTrap amplifies token consumption by $2{,}487.0\times$, $1{,}616.0\times$, and $567.8\times$ relative to a no-token-task baseline for the three workflows. Its router achieves 85.67% accuracy on 300 architecture-labeled prompts. These results demonstrate that short, non-sensitive requests can impose substantial context-processing and coordination costs, motivating resource-aware defense as a complement to scam detection.

title: SARIA: Persistence-Aware KV Caching with Coordinated DRAM--SSD Reload for LLM Agents
authors: Hui Li; Qihui Zhou; Xiao Yan; Shumeng Zhang; Zijie Dai; Zequn Gong; Mingcong Song; Guoping Long; Hongjie Si; James Cheng
abstract: Multi-turn LLM agents usually reuse long context prefixes, making key value (KV) caching crucial for reducing prefill latency. SSDs provide a low-cost extension to limited DRAM capacity but introduce two key challenges. Eagerly persisting all KV cache blocks incurs substantial write traffic and rapidly consumes finite SSD endurance. Meanwhile, the small number of SSDs provisioned in typical GPU servers limits aggregate reload bandwidth, making SSD-resident KV cache much slower to retrieve than that in DRAM and inflating prefill latency. We present \textsc{Saria} (Selective Admission and Reload for Inference Acceleration), a KV caching system that jointly manages DRAM and SSD by exploiting the session-level temporal locality of LLM agents to reduce SSD writes and accelerate cache reload. On the write path, \textsc{Saria} uses eviction and reuse history to selectively persist KV cache blocks that exhibit reuse opportunities beyond their DRAM residency, avoiding unnecessary writes for KV cache already hosted in DRAM. On the read path, \textsc{Saria} promotes selected SSD-hit KV cache blocks from GPU memory into DRAM after prefill, allowing subsequent reuse within the same session to reduce SSD read traffic while limiting DRAM contention. A transfer coordinator paces DRAM reads while SSD transfers are active, allowing both paths to make progress and efficiently share GPU ingress bandwidth. We implement \textsc{Saria} on LMCache MP and evaluate it using workloads from TraceLab and WEKA, covering both full-attention and hybrid-attention models. The results show that \textsc{Saria} reduces SSD writes by 57.1--58.9\% compared with popular full duplicate caching and the mean time to first token (TTFT) by 42.3--79.7\% over DRAM-only caching.

title: UMAS: System-Level Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
authors: Hanwen Li; Jinhao Duan; Xiaoshuang Shi; Yue Zhang; Tianlong Chen; Kaidi Xu; Chenxi Yuan
abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, yet they remain prone to hallucinations and erroneous outputs. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for assessing system reliability, but existing methods are largely designed for single-agent settings; how to exploit MAS structure for UQ while keeping inference cost-neutral remains underexplored. We propose UMAS, a parameter-free, cost-neutral, system-level UQ framework that estimates the credibility of inter-agent influence from each generation's intrinsic confidence. UMAS uses these credibility signals to modulate how uncertainty is updated at each node, and then aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level estimate. Extensive evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show that UMAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 10.54 AUROC points. Beyond uncertainty estimation, UMAS enables hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving MAS accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks while enhancing reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/Dby52-04/UMAS.

title: From Hype to ROI: An Economic Model for LLM Adoption in Information Systems and Security Operations
authors: Pellegrino Casoria; Andrea Araldo; Rosario Patanè; Simon Pietro Romano
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) promise significant efficiency gains across information-intensive operations by automating repetitive language-based tasks. However, adoption decisions remain largely opportunistic, as organizations struggle to move from pilots to sustainable industrialization. Without systematic economic frameworks, practitioners cannot assess whether LLM investments create value in a given context. This paper develops a general economic model to support informed LLM adoption decisions in operational information systems. Facing high uncertainty, we represent parameters as random variables centered on authoritative benchmarks, and evaluate the model by Monte Carlo simulation across pessimistic-to-optimistic assumptions on LLM efficiency. The ROI distributions show the probability of profitability and the Value at Risk for each configuration, together with a sensitivity analysis of its main drivers. As a first instantiation, we apply the model to Security Operations Centers (SOCs), mapping workflows onto established standards to identify tasks suited to LLM augmentation. The model balances productivity gains, driven by alert volume, analyst effort, and LLM efficiency, against operational costs, including inference, infrastructure, and error remediation, covering both cloud API and self-hosted deployments. Results show that adoption economics are context-dependent, and that automation is an exploitable lever, gated by accuracy, while the cost of errors and the model's price are secondary. Across the analyzed models and prices, most configurations are unprofitable, with profitability limited to high-accuracy, low-uncertainty deployments. The model gives organizations a quantitative basis for evidence-based adoption decisions, by locating the boundary between profit and loss, and the loss risked beyond it.

title: DoubleFree:Exploiting Exploration History for Rollout-Free Multi-Task LLMs Training
authors: Yingping Wang; Min Cai; Chenyu Yuan; Xi Ye; Zhijiang Guo; Jiayi Huang
abstract: Multi-task post-training can develop domain specialists through independent reinforcement learning (RL) and consolidate their capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). However, standard MOPD generates on-policy student responses and keeps multiple teachers online throughout consolidation, introducing substantial system costs. We view this pipeline as domain-wise exploration followed by cross-domain exploitation. Domain RL produces not only the final specialists, but also the trajectories collected throughout their training. Existing methods primarily use the former while leaving the latter underutilized. We introduce DoubleFree, which reuses these historical trajectories for rollout-free consolidation and precomputes teacher supervision for online-teacher-free student training. To understand why this works, we analyze when updates from historical trajectories can approximate on-policy distillation updates and how combining trajectories across exploration stages can better support an evolving student. DoubleFree requires only minimal changes to existing post-training frameworks. Across math, code, and instruction following on Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and SmolLM3-3B, DoubleFree achieves $2.99$-$5.75\times$ consolidation speedups and reduces GPU-hours by $80.9$-$90.1\%$, while maintaining comparable multi-domain performance.

title: Synergizing Wireless Foundation Models and LLMs: A Multi-Task Framework for MA Systems
authors: Haocheng Zhang; Yang Liu; Mengzhen Liu; Qingqing Wu; Qingjiang Shi; Wei Wang
abstract: While movable antennas (MAs) provide enhanced spatial flexibility through dynamic repositioning, they confront critical challenges in acquiring complete channel state information (CSI) and efficiently optimizing antenna positions. Encouragingly, wireless foundation models (WFMs) capture generalizable channel priors for high-quality CSI extrapolation, while large language models (LLMs) enable parameter-efficient, token-level optimization for wireless tasks. In this paper, we synergistically integrate a WFM and an LLM into a multi-task framework for MA systems. First, to address the mismatch between existing WFM pre-training and MA channel characteristics, we develop an MA-oriented ``ExtLWM'' based on the large wireless model (LWM) architecture. Second, we design a unified ExtLWM-Connector-LLM architecture that flexibly adapts to different MA configurations without structural redesign. Third, we reformulate discrete MA positioning as a sequential decision-making problem, where candidate positions are represented by numerical tokens and optimized using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to exploit the serial generation capability of the LLM. Finally, a multi-stage training strategy is developed to maintain multi-task performance under limited training samples while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Simulation results show that ExtLWM can produce high-quality channel embeddings while outperforming various benchmarks in CSI extrapolation. Meanwhile, the proposed LLM-based approach achieves a favorable trade-off between performance and computational complexity.

title: MCF: A Memory- and Communication-Aware Co-Designed Framework for Long-Context LLM Inference
authors: Huaizhi Zhang; Jiacheng Zhu; Xuqi Zhu; Junkyu Lee; Klaus McDonald-Maier; Xiaojun Zhai
abstract: This paper presents Memory- and Communication-Aware Framework for Long-Context LLM Inference (MCF) that optimizes long-context inference through communication-aware and stage-adaptive KV-cache layout transitions. At the core of MCF is {Memory-Aware Replication and Scheduling} (MARS), a dynamic orchestration mechanism for chunked prefill. MARS exploits early-stage memory headroom by selectively replicating highly reused KV blocks, improving locality and hiding KV propagation latency behind attention computation. As prefill progresses and memory pressure increases, MARS progressively drains redundant replicas and converges the KV cache into a sharded decode-ready layout, avoiding expensive layout conversion at the prefill--decode boundary. For decoding, MCF adopts a query-centric execution model in which KV shards remain stationary while lightweight query tensors are routed across workers. This changes communication from KV-cache-dependent transfer to query-dependent transfer, reducing communication growth with context length. MCF further integrates a hardware-software co-designed execution layer based on an FPGA compute-NIC datapath, enabling metadata-driven KV routing and collective operations directly in the network path. Experiments show that MCF improves TTFT, throughput, and scalability over state-of-the-art distributed inference systems, with larger benefits as context length and cluster size increase.

title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization
authors: Shuo Chen; Li Cui; Cunxin Huang; Ya-Feng Liu; Minghang Xie; Meng Xu; Zaikun Zhang
abstract: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly to obtain. This setting often arises in simulation-based and experimental applications, where evaluating the black-box objective can itself be costly. Thus, it remains a central challenge in DFO to effectively exploit accumulated observations to select informative evaluation points under a limited budget. In this light, we introduce the NextEval solver, an agent-based DFO solver, which integrates the capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to guide the sequential selection of evaluation points. Specifically, we establish a system that combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment. The environment provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Using observations and tool feedback, the LLM agent selects tools, configures their parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget, while numerical methods compute and evaluate candidate points. Building on this system, we also introduce NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks using the same numerical tools under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems demonstrate that the NextEval solver outperforms the state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.

title: ConfluxServe: Reconciling Resource Utilization and Parallelism Efficiency across Prefill and Decode in LLM Serving
authors: Wenhao Chen; Hong Zhang
abstract: Prefill and decode are complementary in resource usage, but often divergent in parallelism preferences. Executing the two phases separately preserves their preferred parallelism but leaves complementary resources underutilized, while co-batching improves utilization but often requires a uniform parallel configuration that hurts execution efficiency. To resolve this utilization-efficiency dilemma, we propose Conflux Parallelism (XP), a parallel execution abstraction that co-executes prefill and decode with different parallelism within the same batch. Conflux Parallelism exploits operator-level Transformer structure to construct a heterogeneous execution path with different batching and parallelism strategies across operators, combining the best of co-batching and phase-specific execution. Building on Conflux Parallelism, we design ConfluxServe, an SLO-aware serving system that maximizes cluster goodput under TTFT and TBT constraints. Evaluation on production workloads shows that ConfluxServe improves serving goodput by 1.26-1.62x over the strongest baselines.

title: Complementing Text Based Moderation with Multimodal Grounding: Detecting Fraudulent Inducement Behaviors on Short Video Platforms
authors: Xiaoyong Yu
abstract: Short video platforms have become a primary channel for black and gray industry operations in internet finance, where inducements such as prompts to like, follow, join private chat groups, or click external links frequently steer users toward fraud. Because such videos are short, dynamic, and often convey intent through fleeting visual cues rather than stable text, a moderation system must guarantee detection recall and localize the offending segment so reviewers inspect only the relevant clip. Existing OCR+LLM pipelines transcribe on-screen text frame by frame and classify the transcript, but exploit only textual information. Many inducements are conveyed through visual cues OCR cannot observe, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries. We explore OCR+MLLM, which augments the text pipeline with a Multimodal Large Language Model, and compare three routes: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a large zero-shot MLLM, along detection, latency, token consumption, and deployment complexity. OCR preserves the text signal that guarantees recall, while the MLLM jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding, localizing both textual and non-textual inducements. We construct a dataset of 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events across four categories, and study reward design for RL-based grounding under class imbalance. We report two findings: auxiliary reward terms are exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degrade class-balanced detection. We therefore design a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling. Experiments show OCR+MLLM localizes better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline (mIoU 26.52 vs. 14.49) and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss, while maintaining 67.0 percent macro recall.

title: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction
authors: Haoran Bu; Yiting Shen; Litian Zhang; Ruihan Hu; Xi Zhang
abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.

title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
authors: Yipin Guo; Arun M George; Siddharth Joshi
abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

title: FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving
authors: Xin Huang; Teng Ma; Zhuoran Li; Yibo Zhao; Zhaoshi Li; Qianchao Zhu; Wei Yang; Chenxi Wang; Tao Xie; Youwei Zhuo
abstract: KV cache reuse accelerates LLM serving, but existing systems manage host DRAM and NVMe SSD as a tiered hierarchy where DRAM acts as an intermediate cache. Production LLM workloads break both premises of this hierarchy. First, bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering, since workloads are dominated either by one-shot blocks with long reuse distances or by multi-gigabyte agentic sessions that exceed DRAM capacity, putting SSD on the critical read path. Second, DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout bottleneck SSD restoration. Holding host staging buffers for in-flight prefixes causes contention under load that aborts prefetches, while incremental eviction scatters a session's blocks across the SSD and prevents large sequential reads. We present FlatCake, a flat KV storage architecture that exposes host DRAM and NVMe SSD as peer media in a unified 64-bit address space. Exploiting the fact that KV blocks are write-once, immutable, and reused at session scope, FlatCake places each block directly onto its target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order at creation time and never migrates it. FlatCake streams coalesced SSD reads directly into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage and decouples DRAM and SSD request queues to prevent head-of-line blocking. On a production Claude Code trace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, FlatCake sustains a 94% cache hit rate as load increases (versus 64% for Mooncake), eliminates Mooncake's $6.5\times$--$6.7\times$ SSD read amplification, and reduces peak-load mean TTFT by $1.6\times$ while improving total token throughput by $1.6\times$. Across 8K--128K contexts on Llama-3.1-70B, FlatCake further reduces mean TTFT by up to $2.4\times$ over Mooncake and $1.8\times$ over Mooncake-GDS.

title: AgentShield: Fortifying Web Applications Against AI Agents and Agentic Browsers
authors: Moiz Ali; Nafis Karim; Rownak Islam; Jyotirmay Chauhan; Dhruv Kuchhal; Jason Polakis
abstract: LLM-powered browser agents are transforming web automation by autonomously interacting with websites and executing complex workflows. However, the effectiveness of existing anti-bot defenses against these systems remains unclear. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of modern agentic browsers against widely deployed anti-bot mechanisms, characterizing their capabilities, limitations, and behavioral differences from humans. Our results show that many defenses designed for traditional automation struggle to reliably detect autonomous AI-driven agents. Accordingly, we introduce AgentShield, a behavioral fingerprinting framework that targets the Perception-Reasoning-Action (PRA) loop underlying agentic user clients. By leveraging dynamic web forms that progressively reveal content and capture fine-grained interaction telemetry, AgentShield exposes behavioral artifacts that enable differentiation between human users and autonomous agents. We further demonstrate Extinction-induced Policy Drift (EPD), a novel attack in which repeated obstruction of task completion causes agents to relax their safeguards and engage in unsafe behaviors. Finally, we present defensive prompt injection techniques that exploit agent-specific weaknesses to mitigate emerging forms of autonomous web abuse that rely on content extraction. Our results highlight both the shortcomings of current web defenses against agentic user clients and the feasibility of practical detection mechanisms tailored to this new generation of web automation.

title: Prompt Less, Infer More: Static Analysis-Guided LLM Type Annotation for Python
authors: Wonseok Oh; Michael Pradel; Hakjoo Oh
abstract: Type annotations improve the maintainability and reliability of Python programs, but many real-world projects remain under-annotated because manual annotation is time-consuming and error-prone. Recent neural and LLM-based type inference systems can recover missing annotations, yet they often trade accuracy for efficiency. Existing approaches often fail to exploit project-wide type evidence, or do so inefficiently through unnecessary model calls and noisy prompts. We present SALT, an LLM-based type inference system guided by static analysis. SALT integrates static analysis with LLM inference to resolve types statically, prioritize LLM queries, and construct concise type-aware context. To demonstrate the effectiveness of SALT, we evaluated it on 12 real-world Python projects. SALT achieves the best accuracy among the evaluated systems and reduces estimated LLM cost by up to 78.5% compared with a strong coding-assistant baseline. It also shows similar cost savings with the frontier model GPT-5.5, demonstrating that SALT remains effective with strong LLMs.

title: A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development
authors: Leming Shen; Qiang Yang; Xinyu Huang; Zijing Ma; Yuanqing Zheng; Chris Xiaoxuan Lu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit powerful code generation abilities, fostering agentic systems to automate edge AI application development. However, existing agents typically operate via fixed agentic workflows and predefined design spaces, struggling to handle rapidly evolving demands of real-world scenarios (e.g., heterogeneous data modalities, diverse task pipelines). Unlike prior systems that treat LLMs mainly as code generators following rigid workflows, we fully exploit their reasoning capabilities to allow agents to determine their own workflows on the fly. To this end, we propose SE2, a self-exploring and self-evolving paradigm for adaptive edge AI development. Inspired by human learning processes, we distill development into four atomic operations (retrieve, reason, code, test), and empower agents to explore workflows by dynamically and adaptively selecting an appropriate next operation based on the current context. Extensive evaluations show that, with adaptive workflows, the synthesized programs achieve up to 26% higher accuracy and consume 28% lower resources than state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining superior adaptability to unforeseen edge AI scenarios. This highlights the potential of reasoning-driven adaptive agentic workflow in edge AI development.

title: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security
authors: Shiyu Kan; Yue Qi; Yufei Han; Xinjian Luo; Guojun Xiong; Xiaofeng Gao
abstract: Large language model based agents increasingly rely on external tools to invoke services and interact with web resources. These tools can evolve through software updates, yet agentic frameworks may continue trusting them without re-verifying their safety after implementation changes. This tool update gap creates a supply-chain vulnerability in agentic systems: because updated tool code executes outside the LLM's context window, malicious functionality embedded in tool updates can bypass defenses centered on model-visible interactions, leaving agents exposed to stealthy, persistent threats that existing in-context defenses can hardly address. To thoroughly investigate this threat, we introduce ETUDE (Exploiting Tool Updates for Direct Execution), an attack that embeds malicious functionality into updates of initially benign tools to produce compromised tools, while preserving their legitimate tool functionality. Unlike prompt-based attacks, ETUDE operates entirely outside the LLM's context and requires no adversarial instructions, thereby bypassing defenses restricted to model-visible content. We evaluate ETUDE across three representative attack workloads and seven widely used commercial and open-source agentic frameworks, including Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and Claude Code. The results show that ETUDE achieves a 97.6% ASR while maintaining a 95.9% legitimate task completion rate. We further examine existing defenses and find that they provide insufficient protection against this threat. These findings expose a fundamental blind spot in current agent security practices: trust established for a tool does not necessarily remain valid after its implementation updates.

title: Multi-Teacher Reasoning Distillation for LLM Recommendation with Self-Exploration
authors: Liangbo Ning; Siyuan Liang; Yi Zhou; Yifeng Zhang; Qing Li; Wenqi Fan; Dacheng Tao
abstract: Reasoning-augmented recommender systems (RecSys) enhance user preference modeling by generating reasoning trajectories over historical interactions before making recommendations. Knowledge distillation provides a practical paradigm for transferring such reasoning capabilities from powerful large language models to lightweight RecSys. However, existing methods typically rely on a single fixed teacher, remain constrained by the teacher knowledge ceiling, and indiscriminately distill teacher-generated trajectories without assessing their actual utility for downstream recommendation. To address these limitations, we propose MUSE (Multi-Teacher Utility-guided Selection with Self-Exploration), an adaptive reasoning distillation framework that jointly improves reasoning generation and reasoning utilization. MUSE first constructs a diverse reasoning pool using multiple teacher LLMs and progressively augments it via student self-exploration, enabling the student to leverage the strengths of different teachers and gradually explore reasoning strategies beyond teacher imitation. We then develop Rank-Gain Utility Assessment (RGUA), which evaluates each candidate according to the normalized full-catalog rank improvement of the ground-truth item and identifies the most and least recommendation-beneficial trajectories. Based on these utility-aware trajectory pairs, we introduce dual-level contrastive learning objectives that guide the student generator to prefer beneficial reasoning while training the recommendation encoder to more effectively exploit recommendation-relevant preference evidence. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework.

title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
authors: Paulius Skaisgiris; Thomas Pammer; Veronika Semmelrock; Mykyta Ielanskyi; Maximilian Heisinger; Erich Kobler
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.

title: LeanSparse: Memory-Efficient Serving for Native Sparse-Attention LLMs
authors: Zaifeng Pan; Chris Wu; Xinwei Qiang; Zhengding Hu; Zhongkai Yu; Yufei Ding
abstract: Sparse attention limits the history read by each query, but serving long contexts still requires substantial GPU memory. Existing KV offloading systems retain the full history of indexer keys on GPU, limiting decode concurrency. Prefill's temporary memory demand can further delay admission even when enough memory remains for the same request's subsequent decode. We present LeanSparse, a serving system that reduces both decode's persistent memory use and prefill's temporary memory demand. Our design exploits two observations: prefill consumes historical data one layer at a time, and decode can identify promising candidates before comparing their original indexer scores. During prefill, LeanSparse streams layer histories through two reusable GPU buffers, overlapping next-layer loading with ongoing model computation. During decode, coarse-to-fine indexing searches compact representations and retrieves original indexer keys only for candidate refinement. Separate indexer key and KV caches reuse data across generation steps. We implement LeanSparse in SGLang and evaluate it on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. At 950K context length, LeanSparse supports 2.95$\times$ as many concurrent requests and achieves 2.14$\times$ decode throughput over HiSparse. On multi-turn Open-SWE traces, it reduces median time to first token from 21.6 to 0.6s and median session completion time by 17.7% relative to ECHO.

title: Correctness Firewalls for Synthesized Database Components
authors: Mohammad Javad Amiri; Carsten Binnig; Andreas Kipf; Tim Kraska; Ryan Marcus; Johannes Wehrstein; Chenyuan Wu; Geoffrey X. Yu; Zijie Zhao
abstract: For the first time in history, high-performance code is cheap. Today's coding agents can generate bespoke, instance-optimized data systems with excellent performance, and such agents will continue to improve as LLMs advance. But a purely agentic approach, even when validated with strong testing techniques, does not automatically inherit the correctness guarantees our community has spent decades building. We propose a middle ground between hand-crafted and agent-crafted systems: correctness firewalls, lightweight design patterns under which a synthesized component can affect a system's performance but never its results. Behind a correctness firewall, agents are free to synthesize fast components while the overall system remains correct. We present three case studies, each demonstrating a different type of firewall: cardinality estimation (advisory), searching sorted data (guarded), and data compression (certified). In early experiments, synthesized components search sorted data up to 3x faster than human-designed learned indexes and can compress text 1.5x smaller than Zstd. Drawing on these case studies, we outline a research agenda for how data management systems can exploit coding agents without giving up their hard-won correctness guarantees, from protecting synthesized code to measuring the cost of correctness.
